summary: Defines a YANG module for configuring named collections of trusted certificates and trusted public keys. Other data models can refer to these collections when they need to decide whom to trust. The module can also send notifications when certificates are about to expire.

eli5.summary: Imagine a box where a device keeps a list of people it trusts, with their ID cards. This lets other settings point to that box, and it warns you when an ID card is nearly out of date.

questions: how to configure a truststore with netconf
how does yang reference trusted certificates
subtitle: A standard YANG home for named bags of trusted certificates and public keys that other configuration can point to.

tldr.problem: Devices configured through NETCONF or RESTCONF need a common place to hold the certificates and public keys they trust, so that SSH, TLS and other configuration can refer to them instead of repeating them.
tldr.mechanism: The ietf-truststore YANG module defines named bags of certificates and bags of public keys, leafref types and groupings for pointing at them, and a notification that fires when a certificate is about to expire.
tldr.outcome: Other data models can either define keys inline or reference a bag in the truststore. Servers must protect the truststore contents at rest, since the module cannot do that itself.

facts.label: Bag types
facts.value: Certificate bags and public key bags

today: RFC 9641 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2024, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. Related modules for the keystore, SSH and TLS are in RFC 9642, RFC 9644 and RFC 9645.

sections.title: What the Truststore Provides
sections.content:
RFC 9641 defines a YANG 1.1 module called ietf-truststore. It provides a central truststore for raw public keys and certificates, organized as named bags. A bag groups trust anchors that serve a common purpose so that they can be referenced together.

The module also offers types for referencing keys or certificates in the central truststore, and groupings that let a consuming data model choose between configuring keys inline or pointing at the truststore. The truststore can also be instantiated in other data models, in addition to or instead of the central instance.
sections.eli5: It is a filing cabinet for the things a device trusts. Each drawer has a name, so other settings can say 'use the keys in this drawer'.

sections.title: Place in a Family of RFCs
sections.content:
This module is one of a collection of RFCs that together support configuring both clients and servers of NETCONF (RFC 6241) and RESTCONF (RFC 8040). A dependency diagram in the RFC shows the truststore depending on the crypto-types module (RFC 9640), with the keystore (RFC 9642) sitting beside it.

The SSH and TLS client-server groupings (RFC 9644 and RFC 9645) in turn build on the truststore. The RFC also states that it is compliant with the Network Management Datastore Architecture (RFC 8342).
sections.eli5: It is one Lego brick in a bigger set. The crypto-types brick sits underneath, and the SSH and TLS bricks snap on top.

sections.title: The Data Model
sections.content:
The top-level truststore node is enabled by the central-truststore-supported feature and is built from truststore-grouping. That grouping has two lists. certificate-bags (feature certificates) holds bags, each with a name, an optional description and a list of certificates. public-key-bags (feature public-keys) has the same shape for public keys.

Each certificate carries cert-data, a Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) structure that can hold a chain of one or more certificates. Each public key carries a public-key-format identity and the public-key itself as binary data. The grouping exists separately from the top-level node so that other modules can instantiate a truststore elsewhere.
sections.eli5: There are two kinds of bags: one for ID cards (certificates) and one for secret-handshake codes (public keys). Each bag has a name and a short note about what it is for.

sections.title: Types and Groupings for Consumers
sections.content:
The module defines four typedefs, all extending the YANG leafref type: central-certificate-bag-ref, central-certificate-ref, central-public-key-bag-ref and central-public-key-ref. They refer to bags, certificates and keys in the central truststore.

Two reference groupings, central-certificate-ref-grouping and central-public-key-ref-grouping, are provided as conveniences. Two more, inline-or-truststore-certs-grouping and inline-or-truststore-public-keys-grouping, use a YANG choice. One case is an inline-definition (feature inline-definitions-supported) and the other is a central-truststore-reference. More cases MAY be augmented in, for example to reference a bag in another location.
sections.eli5: When a setting needs a list of trusted things, you can either write the list right there or just say the name of a bag you already filled.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC's example truststore defines eight bags: four of certificates and four of public keys. The certificate bags hold trust anchor certificates and end-entity certificates, for authenticating remote servers and remote clients. The key bags hold SSH keys and raw public keys for servers and clients. Real binary data is replaced by the placeholder BASE64VALUE=.

Another example shows a certificate-expiration notification carrying an expiration-date for a named certificate. A third shows two equivalent instances of each inline-or-truststore grouping, one referring to a bag by name and one defining the same values inline.
sections.eli5: The examples show a filled-in cabinet, a warning note saying 'this ID card runs out soon', and two ways to say the same thing: point to a drawer or copy its contents.

sections.title: Built-In Trust Anchors
sections.content:
Some servers ship with built-in trust anchors, for example to reach well-known services such as a Secure Zero-Touch Provisioning bootstrap server (RFC 8572) or to validate public CA certificates for web services. They are expected to be set by a vendor-specific process, and any ability for operators to change them is outside the scope of the RFC.

Because they come from the server rather than from configuration, they appear in the <operational> datastore. The RFC's example marks such bags with the or:origin annotation value or:system.
sections.eli5: Some devices come with a few trusted ID cards already in the box from the factory. You can see them, but they came with the device, not from you.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The name 'truststore' suggests that its contents are protected from unauthorized modification. The YANG module cannot specify controls for data at rest, so server implementations MUST ensure the contents are protected from unauthorized modification when stored.

Public keys are configured without constraints on their use, and trust anchors are implicitly trusted to validate certification paths that may include any name or purpose. Implementations are free to add their own structures and rules to limit a trust anchor's applicability.

The cert-data node uses the NACM default-deny-all extension, and the NACM default-deny-write extension is set for all data nodes, because changing a trust anchor can dramatically alter security policy. The module defines no rpc or action statements.
sections.eli5: If anyone could sneak a fake ID card into the trusted box, the box would be useless. So the device must lock the box, and only allowed people may change what is inside.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA has registered the XML namespace URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-truststore in the IETF XML Registry. It has also recorded the module ietf-truststore in the YANG Module Names registry, with the prefix ts and reference RFC 9641.
sections.eli5: The module's name was written in an official list so nobody else uses the same one.
